evidence.claim: The numbered highway has changed course: from 1926 into the late 1940s, US 68 traveled between Bowling Green and Perryville by way of Horse Cave and Bardstown.

evidence.claim: It shifted to its present routing around 1948–49, apart from the later Glasgow bypass.
evidence.quote: US 68 moved to its current routing between Bowling Green and Perryville (except for the later rerouting onto Glasgow's Veterans Outer Loop) around 1948–49.

evidence.claim: At Pleasant Hill, the Shakers used horses to pump water into a tower in the early 1830s, then piped it to kitchens, cellars and wash houses.
evidence.quote: in the early 1830s the Shakers of Pleasant Hill constructed a water tower on a high plot of ground. A horse-drawn pump lifted water into the tower, and from there a system of pipes conveyed it to the kitchens, cellars, and wash houses.

evidence.claim: Their wash houses also had horse-powered washing machines.
evidence.quote: In the wash houses, the members built washing machines (also powered by horses)

evidence.claim: The community dissolved in 1910, though elderly members remained until Mary Settles died in 1923.
evidence.quote: Following the dissolution of the Shaker society in 1910, the property changed hands several times and was used for a variety of purposes.  Elderly Shakers continued to live on the property until the death in 1923 of Mary Settles

evidence.claim: A restoration effort led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace began in 1961.
evidence.quote: In 1961, a group of Lexington-area citizens led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace launched an effort to restore the property.

evidence.claim: The village now has 34 original nineteenth-century buildings on 2,800 acres of farmland.
evidence.quote: Today, with 34 original 19th-century buildings and 2,800 acres (1100 hectares) of farmland

evidence.quote: In the battle that followed, 60 of the 176 men who followed McGary were killed, Boone's son Israel among them. Another 7 were captured.

evidence.claim: In 1833, Harriet Beecher came to Washington to visit her student Elizabeth Key.
evidence.quote: She came to Washington to visit a student, Elizabeth Key

evidence.claim: Then a teacher at the Western Female Institute in Cincinnati, she witnessed a slave auction in front of the old courthouse.
evidence.quote: At the time of her visit, she was still Harriet Beecher and teaching at the Western Female Institute in Cincinnati.

evidence.claim: That experience, together with her other encounters with slavery, led her to write Uncle Tom’s Cabin after she became Harriet Beecher Stowe.
evidence.quote: This auction and her other experiences with slavery led her to write Uncle Tom's Cabin

evidence.claim: The Key House on Main Street, where she stayed, now contains the Harriet Beecher Stowe Slavery to Freedom Museum.
evidence.quote: The Key House where Harriet Beecher Stowe stayed is on Main Street in Washington and now contains a museum named the Harriet Beecher Stowe Slavery to Freedom Museum.

In 1833, Washington had a visitor who would become famous, Harriet Beecher, who after her marriage was known as Harriet Beecher Stowe.

evidence.claim: In 1830, President Andrew Jackson vetoed a bill allowing federal purchase of stock in the Maysville-Washington-Lexington Turnpike Road Company. The proposed road would have linked Lexington with Washington and the Ohio River at Maysville.
evidence.quote: Washington achieved national attention in 1830 when on May 27 President Andrew Jackson vetoed a bill passed by Congress which would have allowed the Federal Government to purchase stock in the Maysville-Washington-Lexington Turnpike Road Company.

evidence.claim: The proposed road would have linked Lexington with Washington and the Ohio River at Maysville.
evidence.quote: This road would have connected Lexington with Washington and the Ohio River at Maysville

evidence.claim: By 1964, the Friends of Pleasant Hill had secured a $2 million federal loan to buy and restore the property.
evidence.quote: By 1964 the Friends of Pleasant Hill had organized a non-profit corporation, raised funds for operating expenses, and secured a $2 million federal loan to purchase and restore the site.

evidence.quote: Maysville, which was on the Ohio River, replaced it as the largest town and in 1848 replaced it as the county seat of Mason County.

flags: Dropped unsupported current claims that US 68 follows a buffalo trace later made into a Shaker road, and that this drive passes black and white plank fences, horse barns, tobacco fields and limestone fences. The cited foundation snapshot is not in the cache.

The official inventory supports three eastern sections totaling 103.809 miles, a separate 2008 Lebanon–Paducah designation, and separately designated Shakertown Road. It provides no scenic designation rationale. Do not treat 103.809 miles as the whole Kentucky route.

Strip map ends at Lexington, whereas existing landmark moments and the official eastern designation continue to Maysville. Retained these landmarks in eastbound driving order; editorial map reconciliation is needed.
Blue Licks cache does not identify the Indigenous nations in Caldwell’s force. No nation names inferred. It lacks a current museum-access source; no museum visit promised.

Current Pleasant Hill wall-building anecdote is sourced only to an unnamed 1857 visitor. Omitted to avoid unattributed certainty under the prose rule. The Jackson veto is retained without importing a motive.
Washington slavery narrative relies on the cached secondary source; no primary or community source is supplied. Museum existence is documented, but no current opening claim is made.
